items.descriptionOriginal: For decades, India's growing cities have dealt with their waste by moving it out of sight. Over time, municipal dumping grounds have grown into mountains of mixed garbage, often close to homes, informal settlements and roads. But what happens when a city finally clears one of these mountains? Can land occupied by garbage for years become a park, a forest or another public space? And what happens to the people who have depended on these sites for their livelihoods? The Dumpsite Remediation Accelerator Programme (DRAP), launched in November 2025, seeks to accelerate the cleanup of 214 major legacy dumpsites across 200 urban local bodies (ULBs). These sites account for 80% of the remaining legacy waste targeted under the programme, which aims to reclaim land for productive urban use while preventing the creation of new dumpsites by September 2026. The real value of a reclaimed site will depend on what replaces the dump, and how effectively the city manages the waste it generates every. day Photograph: (Needpix) The programme covers 200 ULBs and targets complete remediation of 214 of the most challenging dumpsites across states and Union territories. The scale of the task is considerable, but the experiences of cities already working on or reclaiming such sites show that the challenge extends beyond removing old waste. It involves deciding what happens to the recovered land, where the extracted material goes, and whether the people who have worked with waste for years have a place in the new system. 1. Gorakhpur: A former dumping ground becomes an eco-park In Gorakhpur , Uttar Pradesh, a 40-acre site that had served as the city's primary waste disposal ground for seven years has been transformed into the Kachre Se Kanchan Rapti Eco Park, in September 2026. The remediation involved processing around 400 tonnes of accumulated waste every day. Instead of treating the site as a dumping ground indefinitely, the project sought to recover the land and give it a public-facing purpose. The cleared site was subsequently developed into a public space with green lawns, walking and jogging tracks, a children's play area, an open gym and a yoga zone. Solar lighting and water-conservation structures were also incorporated. According to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the park also has a livelihood component. A women-led self-help group, Shakti Ki Rasoi, operates a restaurant on the premises. The park reportedly attracts around 500 visitors daily. 2. Raichur: Reclaiming a dumpsite for green cover In Raichur, Karnataka, the reclamation of the Yakalaspura dumpsite is taking a different route. Rather than developing a conventional public park across the reclaimed land, the project includes restoring green cover. The 35-acre site has undergone scientific remediation, with approximately 62,252 metric tonnes of waste processed and nearly 22 acres of land reclaimed till 2026, according to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. Part of the restored area now supports a Miyawaki forest spread across approximately five to seven acres. The Miyawaki method involves planting a dense mix of native species to encourage the development of green cover. At a former dumpsite, such an intervention offers a potential ecological use for land cleared of accumulated waste. Planting trees alone does not establish that the land is free from contamination or suitable for every ecological use. Soil quality, the survival of planted species, groundwater conditions and continued maintenance all matter. 3. Delhi: Bhalswa shows why clearing a landfill takes time Delhi's Bhalswa dumpsite offers a contrasting picture. While cities such as Gorakhpur have developed public spaces on reclaimed land, Bhalswa illustrates the scale and complexity of processing decades of accumulated waste. Dating back to 1994, the landfill occupies approximately 70 acres. In June 2022, it held around 73 lakh metric tonnes of legacy waste. Biomining operations began in July that year, involving the excavation, treatment and mechanical separation of old waste into different material streams. By 26 May 2026, approximately 43 acres had been reclaimed. However, around 23.17 lakh metric tonnes of waste, including legacy and fresh waste, remained to be processed, according to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. The figures show that reclaiming a large dumpsite is a gradual process. Biomining involves separating recoverable materials from mixed waste, with different fractions requiring different destinations. Recovered recyclables may enter recycling chains, combustible material may be processed into refuse-derived fuel, and soil-like or inert material may be used for suitable purposes, subject to its quality and applicable environmental requirements. Even after the visible mound shrinks, the land cannot automatically be considered ready for housing, parks or other public uses. Environmental safeguards, including leachate management and fire prevention, remain important, as does monitoring the quality and stability of reclaimed ground. For communities living near Bhalswa, the measure of success is therefore not just the volume of waste removed. It is whether the risks associated with the landfill actually decline, whether fresh waste is managed appropriately and whether the recovered land ultimately serves a clearly defined local purpose. 4. Pune: What happens to the people who work with waste? Pune provides an example of how waste workers can be incorporated into a city's everyday waste-management system. SWaCH, a worker-owned cooperative of waste pickers, enables its members to collect segregated waste door to door and recover recyclable materials. Workers provide a service to households while earning from user fees and the sale of recyclables. The model grew out of organising by the Kagad Kach Patra Kashtakari Panchayat, a waste-pickers' union that has advocated for workers' rights since 1993. Although Pune's cooperative model is not itself an example of a former dumpsite being turned into a park, it offers a useful way to examine the livelihood dimension of remediation. Where new processing facilities are established, cities should assess whether experienced waste pickers can be employed or organised into cooperatives to run parts of the system. Photograph: (Sajjad Hussain/AFP) A 2025 study on Delhi's waste infrastructure highlights a related concern. The closure of traditional waste collection and sorting points, known as dhalaos, and their replacement by compactors or other facilities have affected informal waste pickers, particularly women. Some have had to use their homes for sorting and storing waste, blurring the boundary between their workplace and living space. The transition to a new waste-management system therefore needs to account for the people already working within the old one. Workers need safe working spaces, protective equipment, fair and predictable earnings, access to social security and a meaningful role in decisions affecting their livelihoods. Where new processing facilities are established, cities should assess whether experienced waste pickers can be employed or organised into cooperatives to run parts of the system. The real test begins after remediation DRAP's national target is ambitious, but the scale of the remaining work is substantial. In January 2026, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs reported that 1,138 dumpsites had been fully remediated and 1,020 were under remediation, out of 2,488 identified sites containing more than 1,000 tonnes of waste each. Approximately 15.51 crore metric tonnes of legacy waste had been processed, and 8,484 acres of land reclaimed. These figures indicate the scale of the intervention, but they do not by themselves establish whether nearby residents are experiencing better air quality, whether groundwater risks have declined, or whether waste workers have secured safer livelihoods. The examples from Gorakhpur and Raichur show how reclaimed land can be put to new uses, while Bhalswa demonstrates why remediation cannot be measured only by the visible reduction of a garbage mound. So for cities, the practical priority is twofold: deal responsibly with the waste accumulated over decades and stop creating new mountains through inadequate segregation, collection and processing. A reclaimed site is only the beginning. Its real value will depend on what replaces the dump, how effectively the city manages the waste it generates every day, whether the land is safe for its intended use, and whether the people who have long handled that waste are recognised as essential workers in the process. Sources: 'Dump Site Remediation Acceleration Plan' : By Ministry Of Housing & Urban Affairs, Published On 29 January 2026 'Waste To Woods: Raichur Reclaims 22 Acres With Miyawaki Transformation' : By Press Information Bureau, Published On 18 August 2026 'Pune Civic Body To Complete Biomining Of Waste Dumped At Uruli Devachi-Phursungi Site By 2023 End' : By Ajay Jadhav, Published On 7 April 2023 'Reclaiming The Land Beneath The Waste:Transforming India's Legacy Dumpsites' : By Press Information Bureau, Published On 21 September 2026 'The Intersection Of Waste, Space And Informality: Exploring Spatial And Livelihood Impacts Of Dhalao Closures On Women Waste Pickers In Delhi' : By Shalaka, Urban Studies, School Of Global Affairs, Dr. B.R. items.descriptionOriginal: Whenever Keerthi Krutha's mother, T V Champakalatha, asked her to come home for festivals, she often received an answer that said everything about her daughter's love for the wilderness. "Amma, I am already home. The forest is my home," Keerthi would tell her. For the 36-year-old Chennai-born wildlife researcher, the forests of the Western Ghats had become part of everyday life. After sunset, when frogs began calling from streams and insects filled the air with their sounds, she would set out with a torch, sampling kits and notebooks. Her task was to find the frogs, collect samples from their skin, record what she saw and release them unharmed. Some nights meant crossing slippery rocks and swollen streams. Others brought leeches, unpredictable rain and hours of walking. Yet these were the places Keerthi had always wanted to be. Over several years, working largely on her own, she surveyed 49 protected areas and 19 other landscapes , documenting more than 3,000 amphibians. She was searching for answers to a worrying question: was a fungus that had devastated frogs in other parts of the world spreading through India's forests too? Her research would help scientists understand where the fungus had reached in the Western Ghats and how to keep checking for it. "If frogs are dying, then it means there is a problem," Keerthi told The Hindu in 2015. "Frogs are ecological indicators." Speaking to The Better India , she traces this work back to a childhood spent learning about snakes, crocodiles and forests. It began with a childhood love for wildlife Growing up in Chennai, Keerthi looked forward to nature documentaries and filled her shelves with wildlife books. Family trips often took her to forests rather than popular tourist attractions. The more she learnt, the more time she wanted outdoors. "It wasn't something that came suddenly," her mother tells The Better India . "Nature was always where she felt happiest." Growing up in Chennai, Keerthi looked forward to nature documentaries and filled her shelves with wildlife books. In 2004, as a school student, Keerthi was selected as a Sanctuary Asia Tiger Ambassador through the Kids for Tigers programme. Visits to protected forests introduced her to people who had made wildlife conservation their life's work. Conservation began to feel like a possible future. She also volunteered at the Madras Crocodile Bank, helping clean crocodile enclosures after the 2004 tsunami. While studying for a BTech in Biotechnology at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore, she joined local snake rescues, participated in wildlife estimation exercises and volunteered with conservation organisations. "Wildlife became the direction she wanted her life to take," her mother says. By the time Keerthi graduated in 2012, she knew she wanted to work in conservation. An opportunity soon took her back into the forests, this time to study frogs. Looking for a fungus in frogs After graduating, she joined a project run by the Wildlife Information Liaison Development (WILD) Society and Zoo Outreach Organisation, affiliated with the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER), Pune. The team was investigating a fungus that infects frogs and other amphibians in the Western Ghats. It causes a disease called chytridiomycosis . Scientists call the fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis , or simply chytrid fungus. The fungus attacks their skin, which frogs rely on to absorb water and breathe. In some frogs, a serious infection can be fatal. "It has resulted in the extinction of nearly 200 species of frogs globally and threatens almost 40 percent of amphibian species," Keerthi tells The Better India . The Western Ghats, one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, are home to more than 200 frog species, many found nowhere else. Although India had not seen the mass frog deaths reported elsewhere, scientists had already detected the fungus in several species. "The incidence of this disease was recorded for the first time here in 2011," Keerthi explains. "That made long-term monitoring especially important." Researchers needed to find out which forests harboured the fungus and whether it appeared in new places over time. That meant searching for frogs in the wild, without hurting them. Keerthi was ready to do the work. What it takes to survey thousands of frogs after dark Frogs are especially active at night. Following their calls, Keerthi searched rainforests, evergreen forests, shola grasslands and streams, often working until late in the nights. Even finding these tiny animals could take hours. She carefully took a skin swab from each frog, recorded its details and released it. The swabs could then be tested for fungus without harming the animals. On one of her expeditions, her mother joined her and saw how difficult and demanding her work really was. Between surveys, she stayed in forest camps. Leeches, slippery paths, rising streams and unpredictable weather became familiar parts of the work. On one visit, her mother joined her and saw what these nights demanded. "I realised how difficult and demanding the work really was," she tells The Better India . "But I also knew she was exactly where she wanted to be." For Keerthi, each sample brought scientists closer to understanding the possible danger facing the animals she had spent so long searching for. How tiny skin samples helped track a hidden threat Collecting frogs' skin samples was only half the job. Scientists also needed a reliable way to repeat these checks in different forests and compare what they found. Keerthi helped develop clear steps for finding frogs, taking samples and recording results, so other researchers could follow the same process in the years ahead. Tests at IISER Pune found that the fungus belonged to a type already known to occur widely in Asia. The findings were published in the scientific journal PLOS ONE , adding to what researchers knew about its presence in the Western Ghats. As the work expanded, Keerthi independently secured two grants from the Mohamed bin Zayed Species Conservation Fund. This allowed the surveys to reach more places and the team to continue documenting frogs. The samples and methods gave future researchers a starting point for checking whether the disease was spreading or changing over time. An unexpected discovery in the woods The forests held another surprise. While studying a disease already known to scientists, Keerthi and her colleagues helped identify a frog species that had never been formally described. In 2017, they described Nyctibatrachus mewasinghi , or Mewa Singh's night frog, found only in Kerala's Malabar Wildlife Sanctuary. Discoveries like this help scientists understand where a species lives and which habitats may need protection. But finding a species is only the first step. Understanding the threats it faces is equally important, and frogs themselves can offer valuable clues. Tigers and elephants often draw the spotlight in wildlife conservation. Frogs are easier to overlook, but they can tell us a great deal about the health of our forests. Their skin absorbs water and helps them breathe, making them especially sensitive to pollution, habitat damage and disease. When frog populations begin to decline, it can be an early warning that something is wrong in their surroundings, potentially affecting other wildlife too. "If frogs are dying, then it means there is a problem," Keerthi says. This is what makes her research so important. By identifying where the fungus has been found, Keerthi is helping scientists keep watch for a threat that could affect frogs across the Western Ghats, including species found nowhere else on Earth. For Keerthi, the forest has always been home The child who explored tiger reserves , cleaned crocodile enclosures after the tsunami and rescued snakes grew into a researcher documenting frogs and helping scientists understand a disease threatening them worldwide. Her surveys, scientific work and role in discovering a new species have added to what we know about the Western Ghats and the wildlife that depends on them. Her mother has watched that commitment carry Keerthi through long field trips and festivals away from home. "She has always chosen the forest," she says. All Pictures: Keerthikrutha Seetharaman

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Northwestern University and UC Santa Barbara identified a specific contact point on tau proteins where the misfolding that drives Alzheimer’s disease begins. The finding , published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , suggests the site could be targeted with drugs designed to slow tau tangle growth in the brain. How tau proteins misfold In healthy brains, tau proteins stabilize the internal scaffolding of nerve cells. In tauopathies , including Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia, tau misfolds and recruits healthy proteins to adopt the same abnormal shape. The result is fibrillar aggregates: knotted threads that accumulate and spread through brain tissue. What happens the moment a newly produced tau protein first encounters an existing tangle wasn’t well understood. To find out, chemist Songi Han and colleagues at Northwestern used nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to track engineered tau as it attached to pre-existing tau fibers, watching individual regions as the process unfolded. The region around amino acid 300 stood out because it made contact with existing aggregates faster than any other site examined, acting as an initial anchor. The rest of the protein then aligned to the fiber’s structure. The team calls it “dock-and-lock”: tau docks at the contact point first, then the remaining sections fall into place. Where water comes in The anchor’s stickiness wasn’t fully explained by the protein’s structure. Molecular simulations and water dynamics experiments added a piece: the region around amino acid 300 has an unusual arrangement of water molecules that are easy to dislodge when another tau molecule gets close. That displacement lowers the energy cost of attachment and nudges the docking forward. Chemically blocking the anchor site inhibited fiber growth. Blocking other positions had much less effect. That gap in response is what gives the finding traction as a potential drug target. A possible drug target “Once you know that aggregation-prone tau proteins always have a hotspot that is first attracted to the same site of tau that is stacked to fibrils, then you know there’s always some part of the protein that you can target to neutralize,” said Han. “If you know where to block its action of misfolding, you could block it to prevent it from propagating.” The experiments used a shortened tau construct with a disease-associated mutation, not full-length tau from human tissue , so translation to disease conditions isn’t established. The anchor point’s location may also shift between tau variants and disease types. Whether the mechanism holds across different tau structures, and whether it can be safely disrupted in a living brain, are the next questions. Source study: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences- A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It is harvest time in Kansas City, and at Kansas City Academy, students are stepping outside during lunch to pick jujubes straight off the trees. “I feel like a fairy tale princess every lunch,” said Nova Henry, a senior, “because I get to go out and just feast on little treats.” The trees are free for anyone to take from. That is the whole premise of the Giving Grove , a Kansas City organization 14 years into planting fruit orchards on vacant land and asking nothing in return. It now has 14,000 trees in 847 orchards across 17 cities, and more than a million people live within walking distance of one. The Giving Grove’s origin story The Giving Grove began with a small stand of trees planted 13 years ago on the corner of a shuttered public school in the Waldo neighborhood. The school has since reopened and is expanding, so the original orchard is currently behind a construction fence, but it is still there. “This little orchard we’re standing in here started a national movement,” said Giving Grove Marketing Director Sarah Sikich. “I think it’s one of Kansas City’s best-kept secrets.” From that corner, the organization partnered with Kansas City Community Gardens to spread orchards across unused plots throughout the metro, from a few trees on a school parking lot to plots with over a hundred. Kansas City now has 248 free orchards with nearly 4,600 fruit, nut, and berry trees. “I joke that Kansas City should be the city of orchards, not the city of fountains,” Sikich said. “No other city in the United States has as many orchards as we do.” Built on shared knowledge More than four out of five Giving Grove orchards remain in production. The reason, according to founder Kevin Birzer, is that the organization never just plants trees and walks away. “It’s stuff people can learn, but it takes a long time, and it’s not really efficient for one group to do that,” he said. “So our thought from day one was we would provide that expertise, the knowledge of how to grow the trees , how to select the trees.” About 1,700 “orchard stewards” across the country maintain that relationship. The Giving Grove offers training, workshops, help finding grants, soil improvements, pruning support, and succession planning for when stewards move on or burn out. Janet Porter, a science teacher who tends the orchard at Kansas City Academy, has found the same to be true. “They do training. They do workshops. If I ever have any questions, they’re just a phone call away.” It is not just fruit, either. The trees attract insects , which attract songbirds, which attract predators like hawks. At least one Kansas City student turned pruning experience into a job at a tree nursery. A model spreading city by city Nine years ago, a community gardening group in St. Louis asked for help, and the Giving Grove said yes. Now the organization is in cities across the country, with conversations underway about San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York City. Different communities want different trees, and growing in Brooklyn is not the same as growing in Utah, especially without chemical pesticides or herbicides. “Some environments are more challenging,” Birzer said. “Creating something really cool for the neighborhood, that part’s universal.” The Giving Grove runs on just over $1 million a year. Most of it comes from 1% for the Planet , a network that channels one percent of member businesses’ annual revenue toward environmental causes; corporations sometimes add volunteer labor, and individual donors fill in the rest. The organization only enters communities that invite it, and right now it is working through a backlog of those invitations. “I think people have an easy time falling in love with what we’re doing,” Sikich said. “Planting fruit trees is something everyone can agree with.” Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: A woman flying United from Huntsville to Houston on a Wednesday evening in June boarded the regional jet and found she had it to herself . Under the username u/Sufficient_Fudge_280 , she later posted a photo of the empty plane on Reddit captioned, “Somehow the only person on my flight and the pilot was such a goofy goober.” Somehow the only person on my flight and the pilot was such a goofy goober by u/Sufficient_Fudge_280 in unitedairlines She got her own personalized preflight announcements . The flight attendant also ran the full safety demonstration for an audience of one, laughing the whole way through it. Before takeoff, the crew brought sandbags into the cabin. She wrote that it was “bc the plane was too light with only one passenger,” though that isn’t quite the reason. It’s not that planes are too light to fly, but with an empty cabin, the center of gravity can shift, and that extra weight pulls it back in. On a small regional jet with one person aboard, sandbags are a normal way to solve that problem. A woman walks down the aisle of an empty flight. Photo credit: Yosuke Ota via Unsplash . After landing and taxiing in, the captain invited her up to the flight deck to sit in the seat and look around. “The crew was so cool,” she wrote, adding that the whole thing was funny and joyful. Reddit mostly enjoyed it, with one commenter calling it a “poor man’s private jet.” Another said, “I would have been freaking out at the gate, thinking I was in the wrong place because nobody else was there.” A third quipped, “Still made her gate check her bag for lack of bin space.” The post A woman boarded a United flight and realized she was the only passenger. Then the pilot made it unforgettable. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Ο KC Concepcion ήταν ένας σούπερ σταρ ευρείας δέκτης στην Texas A&M και πολύ γνωστός στους θαυμαστές του College Station. Αλλά όταν μπήκε στο NFL Draft αυτή την περασμένη offseason, παρουσιάστηκε σε ένα εντελώς νέο κοινό που δεν ήταν εξοικειωμένο μαζί του. Σε μια σχεδόν 15λεπτη εμφάνιση στα μέσα μαζικής ενημέρωσης στο συγκρότημα NFL τον Φεβρουάριο του 2026, στέκοντας σόλο στο βάθρο…
items.descriptionOriginal: KC Concepcion was a superstar wide receiver at Texas A&M and well known to the College Station fanbase. But when he entered the NFL Draft this past offseason, he introduced himself to an entirely new audience that was mostly unfamiliar with him. In a nearly 15-minute media appearance at the NFL combine in February 2026, standing solo at the podium fielding questions from NFL reporters, Concepcion’s lifelong stutter was on full display. KC Concepcion has battled ridicule his whole life over stutter In an open letter penned in The Players’ Tribune earlier this year, Concepcion opened up about his struggles growing up with a speech impediment. You’d think being a rising star football player would make anyone immune to bullying, but apparently not when you have a severe stutter. It’s a condition that’s almost impossible to hide in daily life. “The other kids at school, they’d notice how I’d get stuck on certain words. Or that it would take me a second to respond to the teacher, or to tell them my name,” he wrote. “They’d point at me, or make faces, or raise their eyebrows, and then it’d be like…. ‘What’s wrong with you?!??!’ Or ‘Why can’t you talk normal? Are you dumb or something????’ Dead in my face. While cracking up laughing. Not with me , or even about me…. At me. Man … it was tough.” He also writes about how his stutter would disappear “like magic” when he was away from school and not being teased. But in front of his peers, it would always return. Stress and anxiety have been shown to make stuttering noticeably worse. “And back then, how I would deal with my situation is, a lot of times … I’d basically just not talk,” he writes. Star receiver’s stutter remains to this day KC Concepcion still struggles with his speech, though speech classes as a kid helped. His stutter never fully went away. Looking back on his childhood, Concepcion admits that “kids are mean sometimes.” But when he fielded questions from reporters at the NFL Combine in February, he once again faced ridicule from trolls and online bullies. He was in line for a life-changing career move and payday, but instead of soaking up the moment, he felt like he was back on the playground. But this time, he had the perfect response ready. Per Sports Illustrated , Concepcion wrote on his Instagram: “I just wanna say something, if you have a speech impediment, there is nothing wrong with us. I have had this stutter since I can remember talking this is apart of me this is who I am I cannot control this. I wanna be a role model for those who may be scared to speak.” View this post on Instagram Concepcion follows through on his role model promise in the NFL Today, Concepcion is enjoying a solid start to his NFL career as a wide receiver for the Cleveland Browns. But it’s what he’s doing off the field that’s having an even bigger impact. All NFL players are required to speak to the media and perform certain public relations obligations. But Concepcion goes one step further. Despite his speech issues, he doesn’t shy away from the camera and makes a point of speaking on camera every week. At times, the words flow freely out of him. Other times, he struggles with his stutter. But he refuses to fade into the background or hide from the camera. It makes a huge difference for people with speech impediments all over the world. “I wish I had someone like you to represent us stutterers back then. I remember being picked on by adults … for having a stutter and it irked me! I was only a kid, and I still stutter to this day. I’ve always felt insecure about it and I always envy those who can speak fluently,” one commenter wrote on Concepcion’s Instagram. “I learned later on the line that there’s no such thing as perfect speech and having a stutter is ok. Always embrace what you have and don’t let the negative feedback stop you from grinding. You’re a real one.” “You are changing the world on and off the field! As a speech-language pathologist who works exclusively with people who stutter, I see every day how powerful it is when someone speaks openly and unapologetically!” said another. “KC I don’t know you, however I’m very proud of you and what you’ve accomplished. For NOT letting a speech impediment define you. Taking risks and accomplishments that do not go unnoticed,” someone added. “My 12 year old son, who also stutters and has since age 3, had the PRIVILEGE of meeting KC [before a game]. It was an awesome and inspiring moment that my son definitely will never forgot and it TRULY inspired us all!! He told my son, ‘You and me, we’re the same. We go through the same things everyday. But don’t ever let nobody tell you what you cannot do. Be great my boy,'” shared another. It takes tremendous courage and confidence to speak in front of dozens of reporters, with cameras rolling and untold numbers of fans watching at home. But Concepcion finds strength in paving the way for others like him. “So, to any kid out there who is carrying something heavy right now — a stutter, something that makes you feel different, anything that’s ever made someone look at you sideways,” he wrote in his open letter. “Just know this: My success … it is your success , too.” The post Rookie NFL receiver was mocked for his stutter. Now he speaks to the media every single week. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: When a first date goes well , you can tell. It can be as obvious as a consensual goodnight kiss or as subtle as a stolen glance over dessert. Then there are the less obvious tells, like the imperceptible body movements we make when we feel drawn towards a potential love match, and the sound of our voice. Whether we feel a connection during a date isn’t just about what we see, but also what we hear . According to a new study , our vocal cords can reveal our true romantic intentions before we even realize it. These subtle shifts in our voices can show whether we feel a spark with someone or feel compelled to pursue a longer-term relationship. How men and women unconsciously signal interest The study focused on a speed-dating session with 30 single adults, ages 20 to 40 . Afterward, each person reported back on who they wanted to see again. The researchers then examined all the conversations and analyzed each person’s voice. They looked at average pitch, lowest pitch, and pitch variability. The spontaneous shifts in these categories showed a clear pattern. When male participants talked to women they wanted to see again, they lowered their average pitch. This shift became even stronger when the attraction was completely mutual. Men’s vocal timbre also dropped the lowest around women who were popular with other suitors. Women’s voices did something entirely different and surprisingly complex. With men they liked, their voices rose and became more varied. With the men most in demand among other women, their tone dipped lower, but only when they also liked those men personally. Men, in turn, preferred women with lower-pitched voices. A woman’s lowest pitch accounted for up to 55% of the differences in men’s preferences. Overall, subtle acoustic adjustments reveal who we want to impress. The evolutionary reason behind our vocal shifts These vocal changes are not accidental. They are evolutionary tools hardwired into our biology. Women tend to modulate their pitch to better match their social setting. The pitch they use at work likely differs from the one they use with friends or on a first date. For men, dropping their pitch signals capability and strength. Lower voices, regardless of gender, naturally convey confidence, status, and physical presence. A bigger Penn State study backs this up. Researchers had more than 3,100 people in 22 countries listen to the same sentence at different pitches. When asked, both men and women preferred lower voices for a long-term partner. It makes sense that when you’re first meeting someone, you’re looking for quick insights, and how they speak is a fast clue. Context matters, though. Respondents noted that higher-pitched female voices sounded more flirtatious. Men in the survey stated that this vocal variation made these women more attractive to them for short-term relationships. Next time you’re on a date, remember to listen closely to more than just the other person’s words. Pay attention to their voice. Oh, and ask follow-up questions. People like that. The post Researchers discovered a secret vocal signal that reveals when someone is attracted to you appeared first on Upworthy .

Ήταν Σεπτέμβριος του 1977 και η…
items.descriptionOriginal: David Bowie and Bing Crosby were always a bit of an unlikely pair. And yet, they proved that when two incredible talents join forces, a splash of magic can happen. Their story also illustrates that it often takes a village to make a song work, and that was exactly the case with their incredibly popular Christmas duet. It was September 1977, and the air in England was just beginning to turn crisp. American crooner Crosby was recording his Christmas special and had agreed to have David Bowie accompany him on the classic “Little Drummer Boy.” But there was a tiny ripple in the plan. ‘A fascinating combination’ In a behind-the-scenes interview posted on PBS, songwriter and composer Alan “Buz” Kohan (who had also written for Michael Jackson and many other artists) shared what went down when Bowie first heard the arrangement. First, Kohan explained that the production company Smith-Hemion thought Bowie and Crosby were a perfect match. They “figured it would be a fascinating combination, since we were shooting in England anyway, to see if we can get some genuine English performers to appear on the show. And we got Twiggy, and we got some other English artists that were basically only known in England; they didn’t actually translate to America.” Bowie’s answer surprised Kohan. “I don’t know why Bowie said yes, but he did because he was Ziggy Stardust at the time, which is about as far away from Bing Crosby as you could get.” Bowie wasn’t feeling it Only there was a bit of a problem. Kohan continued, “We were going to shoot what was ostensibly just ‘Little Drummer Boy.’ And when we got into rehearsal with him, he said, ‘I don’t really like that song.’ Well, OK, I seem to remember that he said, ‘It doesn’t show off my range now.’ I don’t know if that’s why he didn’t like it or he was just not enamored of it. But anyway, we had this arrangement written out and everything, and the track was made, and everything was set.” He and the writing and music team knew they had a job to do and they had to do it quickly. Kohan shared that he told Bowie, “‘Well, let’s just see what we can do to make it palatable for you,’ and Larry Grossman (composer) and I and Ian Fraser, who was the music director, went down to a little room with a piano. And we decided the best way to salvage the arrangement was to do a counter melody that would fit in between the spaces. And maybe write a new bridge and see if we can sell them that.” ‘Peace on Earth’ was born That is exactly what they did in just about an hour. Kohan continued, “It all happened rather rapidly. I would say within an hour we had it written, and we’re able to present it to him again…We played it for him; he says, ‘Yeah, I like that. I can do that. I think that’s good.’ So he spent about that much time rehearsing it with Bing, and we shot it that day. And that was basically how ‘Peace on Earth’ and ‘Little Drummer Boy’ got married, and we had no trouble picking that up that quickly.” Kohan then explained how rapidly Crosby was able to pick up new material. “He was, in addition to being very articulate, a very bright and aware person. He always knew what was going on around him and he always was able to transform himself without losing any of the Crosby-isms, that relaxed that feeling and the atmosphere that he would always create whenever he was on camera. But he used to love to learn new material.” The collaboration has become one of the most beloved holiday tunes of all time. Though the opening spoken intro might feel a bit forced, the music makes it all worth it. Crosby’s warm baritone traditional parts lie like velvet underneath Bowie’s soul-piercing higher register. It was two voices, two songs, two generations, marinating together like high-end ingredients making the finest meal. Two generations collide Billboard shared a 2014 AP article relaying that Bing’s daughter Mary had thoughts right away. Speaking to a summer TV critics tour, she said: “The doors opened and David walked in with his wife. They were both wearing full-length mink coats, they had matching full makeup, and their hair was bright red…We were thinking, ‘Oh my god.’” Bing’s son Nathaniel added, “It almost didn’t happen. I think the producers told him to take the lipstick off and take the earring out. It was just incredible to see the contrast.” The Christmas special Merrie Olde Christmas was released at the end of November that year. Nearly five years later, RCA released the song as a single. It is still played on radio stations around the world today. A ‘quirky’ idea For his part, Bowie was candid about how strange the combination was. In a 1990 promotional interview , he shared, “The idea I thought was so quirky, it was worth doing. I thought it was an extraordinary situation to be in. And I knew that nobody else would probably do that kind of thing. They don’t, do they?” The post David Bowie disliked Bing Crosby’s duet choice. A last-minute rewrite became a Christmas classic. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Είναι κολίβριο, γεράκι ή σκόρος; Το κάπως συγκεχυμένο όνομα κολιμπρί είναι (drumroll, παρακαλώ) ένα είδος σκώρου που μεταναστεύει στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο και την Ιρλανδία από τη Νότια Ευρώπη και τη Βόρεια Αφρική κάθε καλοκαίρι. items.descriptionOriginal: Is it a hummingbird, a hawk, or a moth? The somewhat confusingly named hummingbird hawk-moth is (drumroll, please) a moth species that migrates to the U.K. and Ireland from southern Europe and North Africa each summer. Its moniker comes from the way it feeds — hovering over flowers like a hummingbird. Wildlife photographer Andrew Fusek-Peters captured that feeding process earlier this month in a series of stunning photos that show the 2-inch insect beating its wings at a staggering 85 times a second while drinking from a valerian bush in his garden in Shropshire, England. Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS The striking moths have been thriving in the U.K. thanks to the warm summer. James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, told the BBC that 2026 was a “record year” for sightings in the country. “They’ve had a really good year this year,” he said. “Normally they would come in small numbers. We’d normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we’ve seen loads of records of them.” Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS Though it borrows its name from the hummingbird, this hawk-moth actually has the avian species beat when it comes to hovering speed — hummingbirds average about 50 beats per second, while the insects can hit up to 85 beats per second. (Another fun fact: Hummingbirds are native only to the Americas, and hummingbird hawk-moths only to the U.K., Europe, and North Africa.) “The hummingbird hawk-moth is a summer visitor to the U.K. from southern Europe and North Africa but can be seen in most months of the year and is a favorite garden visitor,” Fusek-Peters told SWNS. “With warmer summers, it now breeds in the U.K. and will often overwinter here and can now be considered a U.K. breeding species.” He noted that the bugs “emit an audible hum” as they hover. “It means that it can maneuver easily with its long proboscis able to delve into deeper flower stems such as red valerian.” Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS As for how he captured such action-packed photos, Fusek-Peters said it took time and experimentation. “I spent much of the summer photographing them and experimented with slowing down my shutter speed to capture the incredible motion and orange flash of the wings.” This article was originally written by Ed Chatterton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: When some people wake up in the morning , the first thing they do is try to make sense of what happened in their dreams. Whether it was a terrifying night terror where they were pursued by a shadowy figure, or a delightful trip back in time to when they were a child , dreams can affect how we start the day. But for others, they wake up to their alarm and go about their day without even thinking about what happened during the night. It’s as if their brains were wiped clean when they woke up and they never had a dream at all. A 2021 CBS News poll found that 11% of people always remember their dreams, 10% never recall a thing, and the other 79% fall somewhere in between. Why do some people remember their dreams and others do not? A dreamlike state. Photo credit: Canva According to research, people who can remember their dreams have higher activity in their temporoparietal junction , an area of the brain involved in understanding others’ thoughts, shifting attention, and taking different perspectives. “There’s a region in your brain called the temporoparietal junction , which processes information and emotions. This region can also put you in a state of intra-sleep wakefulness, which, in turn, allows your brain to encode and remember dreams better,” Julie Lambert, certified sleep expert, told Healthline in a medically reviewed article . “Researchers also looked at the most common personality traits that are presented in people who can recall their dreams,” Lambert continued. “Overall, such people are prone to daydreaming, creative thinking, and introspection. At the same time, those who are more practical and focused on what is outside themselves tend to have difficulty remembering their dreams.” A young girl having a nightmare. Photo credit: Canva How are people who recall their dreams different? So, if you always recall your dreams, chances are that you are more creative, introspective, and prone to daydreaming. That’s because the temporoparietal junction is associated with the ability to understand other people’s mental states. It also allows us to shift our perspectives from one person or topic to another and pay attention to sudden changes in the environment. This ability to see things from multiple perspectives, easily engage with the world outside ourselves, and shift mindsets is a hallmark of creative thinking. A person with such abilities is more likely to daydream while out on a walk. The problem with people who always remember their dreams While interesting, remembering our dreams has a downside. People who show high activity in the temporoparietal junction may have difficulty sleeping. When that area of the brain is active, it means it’s harder to ignore outside stimuli, which makes it harder to remain in a deep sleep. If you wake up every morning still feeling the emotions of the vivid dreams you’ve had, that shows you are deeply connected to the part of your brain that’s creative and empathetic. Let’s hope those amazing character traits are a decent trade-off for being a little groggy in the morning. This article originally appeared in June. It has been updated. The post People who always remember their dreams don’t sleep as well, but have three impressive qualities appeared first on Upworthy .

Το 2016, ένας υποψήφιος διδάκτορας στο Πανεπιστήμιο της Καλιφόρνια Irvine απέδειξε ότι αυτή είναι όντως η αλήθεια. Πριν από δέκα χρόνια, η Mya Le Thai, PhD έπαιζε στο εργαστήριο όταν έκανε μια κολοσσιαία ανακάλυψη που θα μπορούσε να οδηγήσει σε επαναφόρτιση…
items.descriptionOriginal: A quote widely attributed to the Roman philosopher Seneca says, “Luck happens when preparation meets opportunity.” In 2016, a doctoral candidate at the University of California Irvine proved that this is indeed the truth. Ten years ago, Mya Le Thai, PhD was playing around in the lab when she made a colossal discovery that could lead to a rechargeable battery capable of lasting up to 400 years. That means longer-lasting appliances, laptops, smartphones, cars and so much more, plus fewer lithium ion batteries piling up in landfills . A team of researchers at UCI had been experimenting with nanowires for potential use in batteries, but found that, over time, the thin fragile wires would break down and crack after too many charging cycles. A charge cycle is when a battery goes from completely full to completely empty and back to full again. Phone charging. Photo credit: Canva How the accidental discovery happened But one day on a whim, Thai coated a set of gold nanowires in manganese dioxide and a Plexiglas-like electrolyte gel. “She started to cycle these gel capacitors, and that’s when we got the surprise,” said Reginald Penner, chair of the university’s chemistry department . “She said, ‘this thing has been cycling 10,000 cycles and it’s still going.’ She came back a few days later and said ‘it’s been cycling for 30,000 cycles.’ That kept going on for a month.” This discovery is mind-blowing because the average laptop battery lasts 300 to 500 charge cycles. The nanobattery developed at UCI made it though 200,000 cycles in three months . That would extend the life of the average laptop battery by about 400 years. The rest of the device would have probably gone kaput decades before the battery, but the implications for a battery that lasts hundreds of years are pretty startling. “Mya was playing around, and she coated this whole thing with a very thin gel layer and started to cycle it,” Penner added. “She discovered that just by using this gel, she could cycle it hundreds of thousands of times without losing any capacity.” “That was crazy,” he added, “because these things typically die in dramatic fashion after 5,000 or 6,000 or 7,000 cycles at most.” “The big picture is that there may be a very simple way to stabilize nanowires of the type that we studied,” Penner said. “If this turns out to be generally true, it would be a great advance for the community.” Not bad for just fooling around in the laboratory! Where Mya Le Thai is today Since her discovery, Mya Le Thai earned her PhD and has gone on to a successful career as the Principal Scientist with the Enevate Corporation, a company set “to develop innovative battery technologies that accelerate adoption of electrified mobility,” according to their website. She has also filed patents for her various inventions, the most recent of which being “Cells with blocking devices for delayed heat propagation” in July 2025. As for the original nanowire battery discovery itself, it remains, nearly a decade later, a laboratory proof-of-concept rather than a commercial product. The gold nanowires that made the breakthrough possible are also prohibitively expensive at scale, a hurdle that would need to be solved (researchers have suggested nickel as a cheaper substitute) before this kind of battery could ever show up in an actual laptop or phone. Her full list of patents can be found on Justia . This article originally appeared ten years ago. It has been updated. The post A student accidentally created a rechargeable battery that she says could last 400 years appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment Reading Time: 2 minutes How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment Driving more safely doesn’t just benefit road users. Many of the habits associated with safer driving can also reduce a vehicle’s environmental impact by lowering fuel or energy consumption and cutting harmful emissions . While wider developments in vehicle technology and transport policy play an important role, individual driving habits remain part of the picture. How smoother driving can cut fuel use and emissions According to Energy Saving Trust, efficient driving techniques such as smooth acceleration, staying within speed limits and avoiding unnecessary braking can help reduce fuel consumption and emissions. This means anticipating traffic conditions and maintaining a steady speed wherever it’s safe and practical to do so. Frequent acceleration and harsh braking require more energy than gradual speed changes. In petrol and diesel vehicles, this typically means burning more fuel. In electric vehicles, it can increase battery consumption and reduce driving range. Why speed, braking and forward planning matter Safe driving is closely linked to awareness and anticipation. Giving yourself more time to react to changing road conditions can help reduce sudden manoeuvres that increase fuel consumption and vehicle wear. For example, noticing traffic slowing ahead allows you to ease off the accelerator gradually instead of braking heavily at the last moment. Likewise, anticipating junctions and changing speed limits is key. Drivers looking to improve their awareness may find that utilising telematics insurance to help you be more aware of your driving style encourages more consistent habits, as many telematics systems monitor factors such as braking, acceleration and cornering behaviour. Look after the vehicle as well as your driving style Environmentally responsible driving is not solely about behaviour behind the wheel. Keeping your vehicle in good mechanical condition can also support efficiency and help emissions-control systems operate as intended. Regular servicing allows potential issues to be identified before they affect vehicle performance. Maintaining correct tyre pressures can reduce rolling resistance, while replacing worn components when required can help the vehicle run more efficiently. Drivers should also address dashboard warning lights promptly and ensure emissions-related components are functioning correctly. A poorly maintained vehicle may consume more fuel or energy than necessary. Motoring experts regularly highlight the importance of maintenance as part of environmentally conscious driving, alongside habits such as reducing unnecessary vehicle weight and keeping tyres correctly inflated. Put greener driving into the UK’s bigger environmental picture The UK’s transition towards lower-emission transport involves multiple factors, including advances in vehicle technology and public policy. However, driver behaviour still plays a role. If millions of motorists adopt more efficient driving habits, the combined effect can contribute to lower fuel consumption and reduced emissions across the vehicle fleet. While no individual action can solve environmental challenges on its own, small changes across a large population can support wider sustainability goals. The post How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams Reading Time: 3 minutes How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams Retail teams work across different stores, shifts, and job roles, so training must stay accessible during busy working days. Sales associates need product knowledge, supervisors need management guidance, and every employee must complete required safety courses. A dependable training platform helps meet these demands without disrupting daily store operations. A Learning Management System (LMS) brings these needs into one trackable program. The right retail LMS software also gives leaders a clearer view of participation, assessment results, and unresolved gaps, creating a practical foundation for consistent store training. The following areas outline what to consider when choosing a system. Create One Training Hub For Every Store A retail LMS gives employees one place to access onboarding, product updates, customer service lessons, and compliance courses. A retail LMS software directory helps decision-makers compare systems built for retail requirements, including mobile access, short lessons, progress tracking, and reporting. Centralized content reduces inconsistent instructions between locations and lets training leaders update a course without distributing new files manually. Store teams also benefit from clear learning paths. A new sales associate can complete orientation, point-of-sale training, and product lessons in sequence. A department supervisor can follow a separate path covering coaching, scheduling, inventory procedures, and incident reporting. Deliver Training Around Store Schedules Retail employees rarely share the same hours, making classroom sessions difficult to coordinate. Mobile access lets employees complete assigned lessons between shifts, during scheduled training time, or at another approved location. Short lessons support this schedule. A five-minute module can explain a product feature, customer greeting standard, or safety procedure without removing an employee from the sales floor for a long session. Managers can assign content by role, location, or employment stage, so each learner receives relevant material. A Learning Management System also records completion automatically. Managers do not need separate spreadsheets for each store, which reduces manual follow-up and gives regional leaders a consistent record. Keep Product And Service Knowledge Current Retail information changes often. Product lines, prices, promotions, return rules, and service expectations require regular updates. A central course library lets training teams revise a lesson once and publish the current version across selected stores. Knowledge checks give managers more than a completion mark. Short quizzes can test whether employees understand product differences, warranty conditions, or escalation procedures. Assessment results show where a team needs a refresher before a new promotion begins. Store leaders can also use assigned learning for seasonal hiring. Temporary employees receive the same essential service and safety information as permanent staff, with a clear deadline before their first scheduled shift. Track Compliance Without Manual Chasing Retail organizations must monitor courses related to workplace safety, data protection, harassment prevention, and other internal requirements. An LMS records assignments, due dates, completions, and assessment results in one system. Automated reminders help employees address overdue courses before managers need to contact each person. Escalation reports show which store, role, or department needs attention. These records also give training leaders evidence that required instruction was assigned and completed. Access controls support accurate reporting. A district manager can review assigned stores, while a store manager sees the employees within that location. This structure keeps reports useful without giving every user access to unnecessary information. Use Reports To Improve Store Performance Completion data helps leaders measure participation, but useful reporting goes further. Scores, attempts, time spent, and course status reveal whether employees understood the material or rushed through it. Training leaders can compare results by location or role to find recurring gaps. If several stores perform poorly on a product assessment, the lesson needs clearer explanations or better examples. If one location has low completion rates, managers can review scheduling, communication, or access problems. Learning data also supports regular management routines. Regional leaders can review a monthly report, discuss overdue assignments with store managers, and adjust upcoming training according to business needs. Give Managers A Practical Coaching Tool An LMS supports daily coaching when managers connect online lessons with store activity. After an employee completes a customer service module, a supervisor can observe a customer interaction and discuss the result privately. Managers can assign refresher lessons after an observed gap. They can also recognize completed development paths during one-on-one meetings and use assessment results to plan the next coaching conversation. This approach keeps training connected to job behavior. Employees receive instruction, practice the skill, and discuss progress with a manager instead of treating courses as isolated administrative tasks. Conclusion Retail LMS software gives store teams a shared training structure without forcing every employee into the same schedule. The strongest implementation starts with role-based learning paths, mobile-friendly lessons, current product content, and compliance tracking. Training leaders should audit existing courses, group them by role and store need, then select a system that reports completion and assessment results clearly. A small pilot across several locations provides useful evidence before wider deployment. The post How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable Reading Time: 5 minutes How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable There are events across the entire school/university year for students that cover everything from orientation to graduation, conferences and cultural festivals, sports competitions. These events gather people together, but they also produce extensive waste disposable food containers, printed materials, decorations and single-use supplies for the event. Educational institutions can also lower their carbon footprint by implementing greener practices, because it also teaches students sustainable habits that they will take with them through the rest of their lives after graduation. Sustainable changes to campus events do not necessarily require a large amount of money or radical alterations. Many of the most helpful changes grow out of responsible planning, smart purchasing and greater engagement from the campus community. Think Of Events With Preventive Waste Sustainability needs to be planned in since the earliest stages of planning an event rather than being afterthought once waste is already generated. Organisers can start by estimated attendance, main supplies need to get for use and reference the environmental concern with previous events. Digital registration, electronic invitations and online event schedules are opportunities to eliminate the fabric of waste by cutting out unnecessary paper consumption. For printable materials which are necessary, organizers can print only the copies needed and use double-sided printing when they should be. Also, some schools or universities create sustainability checklists that include catering, transport, energy use and waste management. Clear responsibilities for event teams allow environmentally-sensitive matters to remain part of the planning process. Bottom line prevention from unnecessary consumption tends to work better than fully relying on recycling or disposal systems post-event. Minimize Usage of Single Use Plastics and Disposable Materials But disposable cups, plastic cutlery, food containers and water bottles are other elements of the large waste generated on an important campus meeting. A practical solution would be to offer refill water stations and promote the audience to bring reusable bottles. In places where catering facilities are present, reusable plates, cups and cutleries can take the place of disposable ones. Now when organizing the event, one should count on all the required water, energy as well as cleaning and logistics that are needed to handle reusable items properly. Easily identifiable waste stations are another effective way in which to help participants sort recyclables, general rubbish and food scraps. Such stations would need to mirror local collection and processing facilities available to residents. As there is no appropriate infrastructure, items labelled recyclable or compostable are not necessarily recycled or composted. Prevent unnecessary waste and ensure unavoidable waste is managed properly. Opt For Eco-Friendly Supplies And Materials Another consideration is your event materials. Banners, decorations, name badges, lanyards and exhibition materials are sometimes only used for a limited time before ending up in the bin, even though they can remain in good condition. By selecting durable supplies that can be stored and used again for future events, institutions can minimize this waste. With reusable signage, interchangeable name inserts and returnable badge holders, the need to buy replacements for each event can be limited. Organizers planning student orientations or academic conferences can review the reusable badge and lanyard options available through suppliers such as 4inlanyards when evaluating event identification materials. The broader environmental priority should be to select suitable products, recover them after each event, and reuse them wherever practical. Material composition also matters. Making polyester using recycled PET plastic is a way of reducing the need for virgin polyester, but there are many factors that define the environmental benefits over the whole lifecycle including how it is produced, the length of each product life and end-of-life options. Natural fibres themselves can have environmental impacts involving the cultivation of raw materials, consumption of water, post-harvest processing and transport. Instead of expecting that a single sort of material will always be the most sustainable alternative, institutions should assess durability, practicality, sourcing and end-of-life together. Environmental Initiatives for Campus Catering Food waste is a widespread problem during conferences, student parties and university-wide events. Ordering too much leads to waste, wasting not only the food but also all the resources spent to produce, deliver, and prepare it. By analyzing registration data, organizers can better prepare catering by accurately predicting expected attendance and adapting amounts to the timing of the event. Knowledge, practices and behaviour Change sProviding food that is rich in plant ingredients also can have a positive impact on the environment footprint of catering although this will vary with different components and production methods. Subject to local regulations and food safety and suitability requirements, eligible surplus food may be donated to community groups. Inappropriate collection systems may make even unavoidable food scraps unrecyclable, although these might otherwise be compostable. Institutions can record quantities of food leftovers after an event, which can potentially improve catering estimates for future events and identify sources of recurring waste. Promote Sustainable Transport and EnergyUse Individual travel by car to events over long distances can be a major aspect of the carbon footprint for campus events. Where practical and feasible, universities can promote the use of public transport, walking, cycling and carpooling. Depressingly, taking venues closer to public transport links might also reduce the emissions from travel as well. Energy consumption deserves similar attention. Organizers can have efficient lighting, switch off obsolete equipment, choose rooms according to attendance that are not unnecessarily large and so avoid heating large, empty spaces. Hybrid participation may be appropriate for certain conferences where the reduction in long-distance travel is not outweighed by a disproportionate extra energy use, nor does it exclude people who benefit from attending in person. Such decisions illustrate that event sustainability goes well beyond the materials used on the day. Get Students, Teacher, and the Campus Community Sharing responsibility for being environmentally responsible is what helps sustainable events succeed. Societies on campus, environmental groups, teams from facilities and event volunteers can all help with planning and implementation. They can assist attendees in finding out where they can refill, return reusable items , and sort the waste properly. Student groups can also hold environmental awareness sessions where it explains the reason that such practices are important. Feedback is equally valuable. Holding short post-event surveys can help determine if recycling stations were accessible, if digital materials were available and convenient, and what restatement attendees would support in the future. Participation should remain inclusive. Sustainability programmes must also take account of disabled people, financial inequalities and different access to transport or reusable products. Students engage more in these developments and are likely to continue these routines when practiced. Metrics for Better Future Events Institutions require measurable knowledge to comprehend if their sustainability endeavors are effective. Useful indicators comprise waste generation, food surplus and left over contrary to advice by the industry (i.e.feedback) as well as recovered reusable items and low-impact transportation mode-share. This allows organizers to compare the results of similar events and record which actions made a real difference. It can be something as simple as showing a post-event review that identifies the opportunity to reduce excess orders or enhance waste collection. Environmental reporting should remain transparent. Do not claim that an event is entirely sustainable based on a singular action particularly, as we have seen above where other impacts remain unmeasured or poorly-evaluated. Having a history over time for tracking progress against these targets makes it more likely that schools will set realistic targets and use them to guide decision-making. Final Thoughts Pragmatic choices to reduce waste encouraging printing less, reusing what can be reused again, the selective planning of catering and reducing travel unnecessarily are fundamental ways in making campus buildings and events environmentally sustainable while involving a wider audience on campus. The place to begin can be small steps, monitor outcomes and continuously enhance later on. These initiatives not only lessen environmental impacts but they also create an opportunity to implement practical experience relative to sustainability. Exposure to responsible resource use in everyday campus operations can shape student behavior as they move into their careers and communities. The post How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: At 5 AM, while Kolkata sleeps, a 74-year-old woman is busy spreading happiness, one doorstep at a time. Meet Ratnabali Ghosh, lovingly known as Kolkata’s Alpona Didi. Every year, just before Diwali, she steps out early in the morning to paint beautiful traditional alponas outside strangers’ homes, turning ordinary doorsteps into heartwarming surprises. For elderly residents living away from their children, these intricate patterns mean much more than art. They bring a sense of connection, care, and the comforting feeling that someone is thinking of them. Through this simple yet beautiful gesture, Ratnabali is keeping Bengal’s traditional alpona art alive while bringing smiles to people across Kolkata. Her story reminds us that making a difference doesn’t always require grand gestures. Sometimes, a little kindness can brighten someone’s entire day. ❤️ What is one small act of kindness that has stayed with you? items.descriptionOriginal: "It was given to me in Rs 100 notes, and I remember feeling them in my pocket as I rode my bike back home." That is how Nani described his first salary as an assistant director in an interview Koimoi later revisited, and the sum was Rs 4,000. He has said he felt rich enough that evening to imagine buying half of Hyderabad. Today, the man who counted those notes is Telugu cinema's Natural Star, an actor whom audiences describe as one of the industry's most relatable, and his road there began far from any spotlight. Learning cinema from behind the camera Born Ghanta Naveen Babu in Hyderabad, Nani did not set out to act. Inspired by filmmaker Mani Ratnam , he wanted to direct, and producer Anil Kumar Koneru let him join the sets of Radha Gopalam (2005) as a clap assistant. He then worked as an assistant director on Allari Bullodu, Dhee and Asthram , learning how a film comes together one shot at a time. Nani spent about a year as a radio jockey, hosting Non-Stop Nani before an advertisement led to his acting debut in Ashta Chamma in 2008. Photograph: ( India Today ) But before the camera found him, a microphone did. A friend working at WorldSpace Satellite Radio offered him a job as a radio jockey , and he spent about a year hosting a programme called Non-Stop Nani. According to The Times of India, the show made his voice familiar to listeners, although acting remained his greater ambition. The films that put Nani on the map In 2008, director Mohana Krishna Indraganti noticed Nani in an advertisement and cast him in Ashta Chamma , which gave him his lead-acting debut. The romantic comedy, a free adaptation of Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest , was released on 5 September 2008 and earned Rs 6 crore as the distributors' share, so the newcomer arrived with a success behind him. Ride (2009) and Bheemili Kabaddi Jattu (2010), a remake of the Tamil film Vennila Kabadi Kuzhu, kept the momentum going, with the latter becoming a surprise hit. Snehituda (2009) did not succeed, yet Nani kept getting lead roles, and in 2012 he won the Nandi Award for Best Actor for Yeto Vellipoyindhi Manasu , directed by Gautham Vasudev Menon. Ala Modalaindi , a 2011 romantic comedy directed by Nandini Reddy, became his breakthrough. In 2012, S S Rajamouli cast him in Eega , where Nani's character returns as a fly to take revenge on the man who wronged him. The film earned over Rs 125 crore and won two National Film Awards, which showed how willingly Nani backed ambitious ideas. How he became the 'Natural Star' The nickname arrived with Bhale Bhale Magadivoy in 2015. It was one of the few small-budget Telugu films to cross US$1 million at the box office, and it became the first blockbuster of his career. Nani won the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor in Telugu for it, and audiences began calling him the Natural Star because his performances felt so unforced. In S S Rajamouli's Eega (2012), Nani played a man who returns as a fly to seek revenge, taking on an unconventional role early in his career. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) What kept the title alive was the kind of person he chose to play. His characters are flawed people working through love, ambition, family and the uncertainties of ordinary life, so viewers tend to see themselves in them. In Jersey (2019), he played a former cricketer who returns to the game for the sake of his young son, a performance that Film Companion placed on its list of the 100 greatest performances of the decade. In Hi Nanna (2023), he played a fashion photographer raising his daughter alone, and the film became a commercial success. He also took risks with the image he had built. V (2020), his 25th film and first OTT release, cast him as a serial killer, his first negative role, and it became the most-watched Telugu film on streaming, according to Wikipedia's account of his career. The honours followed. Nani won the Filmfare Critics Award again for Shyam Singha Roy , which made him the only Telugu actor to win it twice. In 2024, he took home his first Filmfare Award for Best Actor in Telugu for Dasara at the 69th Filmfare Awards South, where he was also nominated for Hi Nanna. His next project, The Paradise , reunites him with Dasara director Srikanth Odela. For an actor who once measured success in a pocketful of Rs 100 notes, the journey suggests a career can be built one opportunity at a time, through patience, a willingness to try unusual roles, and a gift for looking like someone the audience already knows. items.descriptionOriginal: With fuel prices sky-high, the need for fuels from non-petroleum sources has taken on a new urgency. And researchers at Worchester Polytechnic Institute say they might have just the alternative source we need for low-carbon and low-cost fuel: bamboo. Bamboo could power trains, planes, and automobiles for as little as $2.75 per gasoline-gallon equivalent at mature commercial scale, the researchers calculate. The fuel would emit greenhouse gas emissions 26 times lower than conventional diesel fuel. What’s more, bamboo promises to be a more sustainable biofuel feedstock than conventional ones like corn and sugarcane. Bamboo is a grass, and one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Some species growing several dozen inches in a day. Because of this fast growth rate, the US could make as much fuel from bamboo as it makes ethanol from corn while using about 13% as much land . The WPI researchers published their results in the journal Sustainable Energy & Fuels . “I think this research is especially timely and important because fuel prices are high and the transportation sector produces more greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. than any other,” said chemical engineering professor Michael Timko in a press release . “Bamboo would use different land than we are using for food production, so there is no food versus fuel trade-off. Farmers win, consumers win.” .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , .IRPP_ruby:visited , .IRPP_ruby:active {border:0!important;}.IRPP_ruby .clearfix:after {content: "";display: table;clear: both;}.IRPP_ruby {display: block;transition: background-color 250ms;webkit-transition: background-color 250ms;width: 100%;opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: #eaeaea;}.IRPP_ruby:active , .IRPP_ruby:hover {opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: inherit;}.IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl {background-position: center;background-size: cover;float: left;margin: 0;padding: 0;width: 31.59%;position: absolute;top: 0;bottom: 0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {float: right;width: 65.65%;padding:0;margin:0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text {display: table;height: 130px;left: 0;top: 0;padding:0;margin:0;padding-top: 20px;padding-bottom: 20px;}.IRPP_ruby .IRPP_ruby-content {display: table-cell;margin: 0;padding: 0 74px 0 0px;position: relative;vertical-align: middle;width: 100%;}.IRPP_ruby .ctaText {border-bottom: 0 solid #fff;color: #0099cc;font-size: 14px;font-weight: bold;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .postTitle {color: #000000;font-size: 16px;font-weight: 600;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .ctaButton {background: url(https://www.anthropocenemagazine.org/wp-content/plugins/intelly-related-posts-pro/assets/images/next-arrow.png)no-repeat;background-color: #afb4b6;background-position: center;display: inline-block;height: 100%;width: 54px;margin-left: 10px;position: absolute;bottom:0;right: 0;top: 0;}.IRPP_ruby:after {content: "";display: block;clear: both;} Recommended Reading: How sustainable are aviation biofuels really? Timko and colleagues evaluated bamboo for biofuel production using a process called hydrothermal liquefaction. In the process, wet biomass or organic wastes are subjected to high heat and pressure. Polymer chains in the mass breaks down to form a biocrude oil. The oil can then be converted to other liquid fuel products. The researchers heated wet bamboo pulp to 300°C for 10 minutes. The process converted about 36% of its mass into biocrude. Unlike corn or sugarcane, which are the main plants used to make biofuels today , bamboo wouldn’t compete with agricultural land and doesn’t need much water or energy to grow. And compared with other perennial grasses that are also being considered for biofuel, it has very low ash content—less than 1% by weight—so the fuel-making process generates minimal waste. ”Bamboo may eventually offer industry a way to generate low-carbon liquid fuels at scale,” Timko said. Source : Timothy M. Woodard et al. Bamboo as a cost-effective feedstock for production of low carbon transportation fuels. Sustainable Energy & Fuels , 2026.
