items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips Reading Time: 3 minutes Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Suppliers and Buying Tips If you’re wondering, “Where can I buy peppermint oil in bulk?”, you have many options, including specialist wholesalers, ingredient distributors, and online marketplaces. Wholesale Botanics, Bulk Apothecary, and Bulk Natural Oils are just a few options worth considering. Walmart also lists larger bottles, while Amazon is another marketplace to check. The best starting point depends on the quantity of the product you need. A larger bottle may suit occasional soap making, but regular production calls for a reliable supplier. Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Specialist Suppliers for Bulk Peppermint Oil Consider these suppliers if you’re looking to buy peppermint oil in bulk. Wholesale Botanics Wholesale Botanics lists peppermint oil in 5, 25, 100, and 400-pound sizes, with custom quotes for larger quantities. Buyers have the option to choose between Mentha piperita and Mentha arvensis variants. Wholesale Botanics’ essential oil wholesale service offers consultations and sample packs, enabling you to discuss requirements before placing an order. You can also request a sample of the variant you want to purchase and confirm that testing documents are also provided. Bulk Apothecary Bulk Apothecary offers Japanese and Supreme peppermint oils in 5, 25, and 400-pound options. Shipping is calculated at checkout, so bear that in mind when purchasing. The smaller bottles allow you to test a variety before moving to a larger order. It helps to ask the company’s team about quantities beyond the listed options. New Directions Aromatics New Directions Aromatics offers its Peppermint Essential Oil (Supreme) in sizes that extend up to 396 pounds. This is the Mentha piperita variation, but it also has organic peppermint listings. Availability and dispatch arrangements differ between sizes, so it helps to confirm the selected pack is available. Bulk Natural Oils Bulk Natural Oils offer Piperita and Arvensis peppermint oils as well as organic options. The website lists a minimum spend of $150 on a combination of products. This option might suit businesses purchasing several ingredients together. Shay and Company Shay and Company is a good choice for smaller buys as it offers peppermint oil in smaller bottles in 5- and 10-pound sizes. Orders over 25 pounds require an email inquiry. Its Willamette Valley listing identifies Oregon as the origin, making it worth exploring when sourcing location matters to your product. Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? Can You Buy on Amazon or Walmart? Walmart’s online listings include peppermint oil in 16-ounce bottles as well as one-gallon containers. This might suit smaller projects that don’t have a large wholesale commitment. Ensure that you check the individual seller, ingredients, and documentation instead of relying on the retailer’s name alone. If you want to purchase peppermint oil on Amazon, search for the quantity you need and check who sells and ships the product. Double-check that the listing describes essential oil and not fragrance oil, extract, or a diluted blend. Check the Oil Before Comparing Prices You would typically come across two main variants: Mentha piperita, which is peppermint, and Mentha arvensis, commonly called cornmint or Japanese peppermint. While both appear in peppermint ranges, their aromas and chemical profiles differ. Make sure that you match the botanical name to your formula instead of substituting whichever costs less. Where possible, request a certificate of analysis, an available batch-specific GC/MS report, and a safety data sheet. These cover specifications, handling hazards, and chemical composition. Request the relevant certification and confirmation of suitability for certified organic, food, or oral care application. Remember that “pure” alone doesn’t establish that an oil meets your requirements. Compare Delivered Cost and Order Size In your comparison between products, factor in shipping, taxes, import charges, and membership fees. Check whether the ounces refer to weight or fluid volume. For international orders, check that the selected quantity can actually be shipped to your country and clearly establish who pays the customs charges. Drum deliveries can involve freight shipping, so ask about unloading requirements as well. For occasional purchases, compare membership savings with subscription costs before signing up for a wholesale plan. Always test a sample in the finished product before scaling up, as peppermint oil can irritate skin, and cosmetics and candles require appropriate safety or performance testing. Confirm lead times, return conditions, and remaining shelf life before paying. Store the oil tightly sealed, away from heat and light, and order only what you can realistically use. Choosing Where to Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk Amazon and Walmart are worth exploring if you want to purchase a large bottle as a one-time thing. For regular production, specialist suppliers give you more options to discuss specifications and quantities. Start by requesting a sample and a quote for the oil you need. Once you test it in your formula, you can decide whether the pricing, documentation, and availability make it a practical choice for future orders. The post Where Can I Buy Peppermint Oil in Bulk? items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers in Spain have shown that a modular tire in which tread and casing are designed as separate pieces stays together while in use, provided that it’s properly inflated. “This is an encouraging step toward a more sustainable tire architecture, where the worn tread could potentially be replaced while the main tire structure is reused,” says study team member Farshad Afshari , a PhD researcher at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M) and Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (UPM).. A modular automobile tire could be easier to recycle compared to conventional ones, which require time- and labor-intensive separation of rubber treads and sidewalls from steel belts and bead cores. It would also use materials more efficiently, since there would be less material to replace at any given time. A modular tire could also be better for the environment . Conventional rubber tires are a prominent source of microplastic pollution because tiny rubber particles degrade due to friction and enter the air and waterways. But the modular design could open up the possibility of making each component of the tire from safer and more easily recyclable materials. It’s a compelling idea in theory, but would the components of a modular tire actually stay together in practice? Afshari and his collaborators built a scaled-down prototype of their ECOTIRE modular tire concept, in which tread and casing are mechanically interlocked through a series of bumps and hollows like the two halves of a waffle iron. They tested the tire on a custom-built rolling test rig in the lab to see how the tire would fare while varying parameters such as load, turning radius, inflation pressure, and slip. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Greening Upwind of Cities Could Cool Megacities by Nearly Half a Degree Reading Time: 3 minutes Greening upwind of cities may offer a simple fix for urban heat, with new research showing strategically placed suburban forests can cool more than half a metropolitan area. Greening upwind of cities draws on a centuries-old planning idea. Researchers behind the new study found inspiration in traditional Chinese village design , where settlements were built backed by mountains, facing water, and surrounded by forest. That layout, known as the mountain-water-forest framework, helped villages stay naturally cooler. Shi-Jie Cao, director of the Center for Sustainable Built Environment at Southeast University in Nanjing, led the team exploring whether this ancient pattern could work for modern megacities. Many cities have already tried planting trees within urban cores to combat heat. Results have often fallen short, leaving some cities sweltering through increasingly hot summers despite those efforts. Cao’s team wondered if location mattered more than volume. Placing vegetation strategically outside a city, rather than scattering it inside, might produce better cooling results. Testing that idea required a different approach than simply counting trees planted downtown. Researchers built a computer model to simulate temperature changes in urban cores during hot summer days. They tested what would happen if suburban land upwind of two Chinese cities, Beijing and Shanghai, were converted into either forest or built-up development. The two cities offered contrasting geography, with Beijing sitting on a plain near mountains and Shanghai positioned along the coast. Results revealed a clear mechanism. Greening upwind of cities creates a mass of cooler air in the surrounding suburbs. Prevailing winds then carry that cooler air directly into the city, lowering temperatures across the urban core without requiring any changes inside city limits. Encouraged by these findings, researchers expanded their analysis to six additional megacities worldwide. Cairo, Kinshasa, São Paulo, Houston, Sydney, and London each represent vastly different climates and urban layouts. Testing across such varied conditions helped determine whether the cooling strategy held up beyond China’s borders. Across all eight cities studied, greening upwind of cities produced an average cooling effect of 0.4 degrees Celsius. That temperature drop applied across at least half of each city’s total area during peak summer heat. Exact results varied by location, but the underlying cooling pathway remained consistent everywhere researchers tested it. A city skyline rises beyond green suburban land, illustrating the wind pathway researchers studied when greening upwind of cities to reduce heat. Photo by Andy Lee on Pexels. Shanghai’s results illustrated the strategy’s limits alongside its potential. Cooling effects there were more modest and localized than in Beijing. Shanghai’s cooling sea breezes simply don’t align well with the areas where suburban trees could realistically be planted, reducing how effectively wind carries cooled air into the city. That finding carries an important caveat for city planners. Cao emphasized that this approach isn’t a blanket call for planting trees everywhere possible. Success depends on cities having consistent wind patterns and available space specifically positioned upwind of urban centers. Available space presents its own complication in many real-world settings. Suburban land upwind of major cities often already hosts housing developments, roads, and industrial facilities. Implementing this strategy would require creative, multi-functional land-use planning rather than simply clearing space for new forests. Local governments and other stakeholders would need to coordinate closely to make such changes possible. Getting buy-in across multiple jurisdictions and property owners adds real-world complexity that no climate model can capture. Political and logistical hurdles may prove just as challenging as the science itself. Beyond the specific temperature findings, Cao pointed to a broader lesson drawn from traditional village design. Cities benefit from thinking about vegetation, wind, topography, and water as one interconnected system rather than isolated green spaces scattered without coordination. That systems-level thinking represents a meaningful shift from how most urban cooling efforts currently operate. As global temperatures continue rising, cities will likely need every available tool to manage heat exposure for residents. Greening upwind of cities offers city planners a research-backed strategy that works with existing wind patterns rather than against them. The approach won’t work everywhere, but where geography cooperates, it could meaningfully ease the burden of urban heat without requiring dramatic changes to how city centers themselves are built. The post Greening Upwind of Cities Could Cool Megacities by Nearly Half a Degree appeared first on Happy Eco News .

W hen I was a student at Cornell University, I read the book “Fraternity Gang Rape” by Peggy Reeves Sanday for one of my classes. That book was written in 1990, which was a long time ago. But then again, was it? I took the book off my shelf today. Paging through it, I noticed a sickening pattern. Parts of it felt ripped from the allegations coming out of the Cornell investigation today: Long nights saturated in alcohol. Women who spend days tunneling through layers of self-blame and shame before concluding they’ve been raped. Prosecutors who do not pursue charges. One example: a 19-year-old woman at a small Midwestern college drank alcohol, had sex with her boyfriend, “fell asleep and the next thing she knew she awoke with a man she didn’t know on top of her.” The more things change, apparently, the less any goddamn thing changes. But wait. At moments of despair like this, I have learned to stop and ask myself: Is it actually true that nothing has changed? There has been some extraordinary reporting done about the Cornell case, including by The Cornell Daily Sun , the student-run newspaper that gave me my first reporting job many years ago. But as usually happens with terrifying news stories, it’s very hard to figure out how to assess the threat — and find proven solutions. How typical was this case? Is sexual assault happening more or less over time? In other words, what is the denominator for whatever fresh horror we are worried about? Most importantly, what actually works to make sexual assault more rare? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] To answer these questions, I’m going to uncomfortably set aside many other important questions — about accountability, humanity, legality, fairness and barbarity. Those are questions being interrogated in many other places. Here at The Understory, we’re trying to fill gaps that we see in traditional journalism. And one of those gaps is almost always context: How often are horrible things happening, and what can be done to make them more rare? These are the kinds of questions that we know humans need answered, in order to stay sane and take meaningful action in a time of relentless news battering us from near and far. So in that spirit, here is what I have learned so far: Rape reports have been declining in the U.S. since 2021. For 2025, the FBI estimates that 36 rape offenses were reported for every 100,000 people. The number of rapes that get reported to law enforcement each year has been gradually declining every year since 2021 , based on FBI data. This data comes with giant caveats, though. First, the number of actual sexual assaults is far higher than the number that get reported. (Only about 24 percent of sexual assaults were reported to authorities in 2024, according to the National Crime Victimization Survey .) Second, the FBI broadened its definition of rape in 2013, so it is hard to compare statistics going back any further than that. (The current definition includes “penetration, no matter how slight, of the vagina or anus with any body part or object, or oral penetration by a sex organ of another person, without the consent of the victim.”) In general, definitions of rape and sexual assault vary from place to place, making it harder than it should be to track changes over time and to find which cities, states or countries have unusually low (or high) rates. Sexual assault remains appallingly common on college campuses. In 2019, 13 percent of college students reported that they’d experienced some form of sexual assault since they’d arrived on campus. This category is broader than the FBI definition of rape; it includes nonconsensual penetration, attempted penetration, sexual touching by force or inability to consent. This data comes from the 181,752 students who responded to the 2019 Campus Climate Survey (conducted by the Association of American Universities). Importantly, the odds vary tremendously depending on who you are. The rate of sexual assault for women and transgender or nonbinary students was 20 percent — or four times the rate for men. Credit: Zhuoyao Song / Shutterstock The Cornell case is typical in some ways. In most campus sexual assaults, both the victim and the offender have consumed alcohol or drugs. Typically, rape victims are girls and very young women, and the vast majority of perpetrators are male. Victims usually know their perpetrators. At colleges, assaults primarily happen in residences or fraternity houses, according to the Campus Climate Survey (and Cornell’s own 2025 survey on sexual assault). And if a victim reports the offense, official responses are slow and unsatisfying, generally speaking. In all these ways, the Cornell case seems fairly typical. The Cornell case is atypical in other ways. Most sexual assault cases involve just one perpetrator, not multiple, making the Cornell allegations unusual. The other rarity is that the woman in this case reported the incident. And she has continued to push for a reckoning in a civil suit filed this year. To date, none of the accused men has been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing. Something can be done. And is being done. There is a lot of speculation happening right now about what leads to rape. Can we blame always-accessible, violent porn? Or campus hookup culture and frat-boy privilege? I have hunches about this, like everyone else. But I’m more interested in evidence of change. What actually works to reduce the number of rapes? And guess what? We now have some answers — answers we did not have when I was a student at Cornell. A 2014 study led by Laura Salazar at Georgia State University randomly assigned 743 college men to receive something called the RealConsent online training or a generic online health program. RealConsent featured six 30-minute modules about informed consent, intimate communication skills, the role of alcohol and male socialization in sexual violence, empathy for rape victims and bystander education. Six months later, the men who had received the special training reported intervening more often to stop a peer from engaging in sexually violent or inappropriate behavior. And, most importantly, they reported engaging in less sexual aggression themselves. “The odds for perpetrating among RealConsent participants were 73 percent lower than participants in the comparison condition,” according to the study. The attitudes of these men changed, too. They had greater empathy for rape victims, less hostility toward women and less comfort with other men’s inappropriate behaviors. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Another program, which has been studied even more extensively, first appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine in 2015. The researchers, led by Charlene Senn at the University of Windsor, randomly assigned a group of first-year female students at three Canadian universities to receive a special training program for resisting sexual assault. The control group got general brochures on sexual assault instead. The training program, known as EAAA (for Enhanced Assess, Acknowledge, Act) featured four three-hour sessions. Students were taught how to assess risk, overcome emotional barriers in acknowledging danger and engage in effective verbal and physical self-defense. In all, 451 women received the EAAA training, and 442 women got the brochures. One year later, the researchers checked in on the women. Get this: women in the training group were 46 percent less likely to report having been raped than women in the control group. They were also 63 percent less likely to report attempted rapes. A subsequent study found that the benefits continued, even two years later. “The program significantly reduced the risk of completed and attempted rape, attempted coercion, and nonconsensual sexual contact over the entire follow-up period,” the study concluded, “yielding reductions between 30 percent and 64 percent at 2 years.” Women who still became victims of sexual violence, despite the training, were less likely to blame themselves than women in the control group. The U.S. Air Force Academy has adopted the program for first-year female cadets. So have many colleges, including Stanford University. Interestingly, Cornell University has tried out this program, too. Cornell facilitators piloted the EAAA program in 2019 and 2020. Then the pandemic came along and on-campus training stopped . Which means it’s unlikely that the students involved in the 2024 case got this training. Last year, Cornell revived the EAAA program with sorority members, as well as a parallel program for fraternity members. You might wonder: Why isn’t every high school student getting proven training like this? There are many reasons, but one reason is that too few people know about these options. When rapes get covered in the media, the reporting almost never includes research like this. It can feel like this kind of violence is inevitable — or the fault of some inherent flaw in the perpetrators. But violence is never inevitable. We, as a society, tend to focus on holding perpetrators accountable after the fact. And this is important, but tragically late. It would be great if laws were clearer, data collection was consistent and police and prosecutors had excellent, trauma-informed training. But it would be infinitely better to prevent more rapes from happening at all. “Despair demands less of us, it’s more predictable, and in a sad way safer,” Rebecca Solnit wrote in Hope in the Dark. “Authentic hope requires clarity — seeing the troubles in this world — and imagination, seeing what might lie beyond these situations that are perhaps not inevitable and immutable.” The post There Are Ways to Reduce Campus Sexual Assaults. Will More Colleges Use Them? appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.titleOriginal: He Wanted Kids To Understand Cancer. So He turned It Into A Game
items.description: Όταν ο Daniel Zhang ήταν εννέα, είδε τη γιαγιά του να χάνει τα μαλλιά της λόγω χημειοθεραπείας και δεν μπορούσε να καταλάβει γιατί η ιατρική μπορούσε να μοιάζει τόσο πολύ με κακό. Αυτή η σύγχυση δεν τον εγκατέλειψε ποτέ, και όταν αργότερα ο παππούς του διαγνώστηκε με καρκίνο -- και ο Ζανγκ είδε την ίδια σύγχυση στο πρόσωπο της επτάχρονης αδερφής του -- έγινε ο σπόρος του…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Daniel Zhang was nine, he watched his grandmother lose her hair to chemotherapy and couldn't understand why medicine could look so much like harm. That confusion never left him, and when his grandfather was later diagnosed with cancer -- and Zhang saw the same bewilderment on his seven-year-old sister's face -- it became the seed of something purposeful. He and his classmate Zachary Tou, both 17, built *Tumor Tactics*, a Pok mon-inspired card game that teaches children cancer biology through the same mechanics they already love -- where, as Zhang explains, "chemotherapy can be a really powerful treatment, but you have to roll a die to determine how effective it is, and you might have to skip your next turn to recover from its side effects." What began as one boy trying to translate grief into language a child could hold has grown into a student-led nonprofit running workshops across San Diego schools, reaching kids from kindergarten through eighth grade. Perhaps most quietly remarkable is what happens at the end of each session: Zhang and Tou open the floor for discussion, and children -- unbidden -- begin sharing their own family stories, needing not just explanation, but the invitation to be heard.

items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Peter McGraw, καθηγητή μάρκετινγκ και ψυχολογίας στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Colorado Boulder, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Τα σόλο ταξίδια αυξάνονται — και μια βιομηχανία…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Peter McGraw , a professor of marketing and psychology at the University of Colorado Boulder, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Solo travel is surging — and an industry still largely built for two is taking note. Google reported in April 2026 that online searches involving “solo travel” hit an all-time high this year, with queries for “women solo travel” reaching a 15-year peak. Hilton’s 2026 trends report found that 26% of travelers planned to take a trip alone this year, and that nearly half said they planned to add solo days to the front or back of a family trip. The issue isn’t new. In 1992, marketing researchers identified the solo consumer as an underserved market . But as tourism researchers have documented , the accommodation sector treats double occupancy as the default unit of consumption, which often slaps a “single supplement” charge on customers when they travel without a partner. The industry essentially penalizes travelers for arriving without a second body to fill the other half of a room they aren’t using. The reason why so many hotels, cruise lines, and tour operators still base prices on double occupancy is that their costs — the room, the berth, the coach seat, the guide — don’t fall by half when the second person fails to materialize. But the supplement isn’t just a pricing convention. It’s the clearest signal the industry sends about who it built the product for. I’m a scholar who studies what I call the solo economy : how institutions and markets adapt, or fail to adapt, to the rise of single living. I’ve written before about how retail and restaurants still design for pairs. Travel is further along than most in recognizing this cultural shift. It’s also a useful case because the industry has started on the easy part of the problem but barely touched the rest. Demographics Matter, but Not the Way You’d Think The broader shift toward solo living is real. In 2025, 39.7 million Americans lived alone . That’s 29% of all households, up from 20% in 1975. Married couples, meanwhile, fell to 47% of households from 66% 50 years earlier. Those numbers alone don’t explain solo travel. Some of that decline went to people living alone; some went to unmarried couples, who are still a party of two on a booking page. Married people take trips alone. Single people travel with friends, siblings and parents, and plenty of them have logged serious hours as an extra wheel. Living alone and vacationing alone are different behaviors with different causes. What connects them is the erosion of a single assumption: that every adult arrives with a plus-one. That assumption is weakening at home, and it’s now encountering the booking page. Price Is the Easy Rung One response by the travel industry has been to shave the single supplement. For example, the tour operator Tauck announced this year that it’s waiving the single supplement on a class of its riverboat cabins across more than 250 European river cruise departures and reducing it by up to US$600 on 105 land departures. Another touring company has taken a more committed approach to adjusting its offerings: Aurora Expeditions sets aside 10 dedicated solo cabins on every sailing across its three ships, with no single supplement, through its 2026 and 2027 seasons. Then there’s Norwegian Cruise Line, which was early to the shift. In 2010, it introduced Studio staterooms aboard Norwegian Epic: small cabins designed for one passenger, sold at single-occupancy prices and arranged around a keycard-access Studio Lounge reserved for solo travelers. The trade-off is less private space, but at a price for one, with access to a room full of fellow travelers going it alone. Norwegian then expanded solo categories in 2024 from nine ships to its full 19-ship fleet. But on ships without Studios, much of the expansion was relabeling. Cruise Critic reported that standard double-occupancy rooms would likely be reclassified rather than retrofitted. And by Norwegian’s own account , the Studio Lounge is reserved for guests in Solo Studios — so the fleetwide solo categories come with the discount but not the room full of other solo travelers. That’s the difference between repricing and redesigning. The 2010 Studio was a purpose-built 100-square-foot (9 square-meter) cabin that cost Norwegian something to construct. The 2024 categories are, in many cases, the same rooms as before, with a new label and a discount. The solo traveler pays less than two people would, but it’s still more than half for a room sized and built for two. A cabin sold to one occupies the same space as a cabin sold to two, and the industry still counts berths. There’s a cleaner approach. Yotel sells a room type it calls Solo — 114 square feet (about 10 square meters) in New York City, maximum occupancy one, at the bottom of its price range. Nothing was subtracted to make it. It was built at that size, for that guest, and priced accordingly. That’s what designing for one looks like, and it’s rare enough that a tiny room counts as progress. alvarez—E+/Getty Images Many solo travelers seek control over their experiences and schedules, but they still seek a social component. Traveling Alone Doesn’t Mean Being Alone A common mistake in designing for solo travelers is assuming that solitude is the product. It isn’t. In the same 2026 data showing record interest in solo travel, Google found that searches for “travel groups” and “tour groups” also hit record highs . A Mastercard survey of more than 15,000 consumers across 11 countries found that 39% of international travelers had already taken a trip alone — and 7 in 10 international leisure travelers were interested in solo experiences built to connect them with like-minded people. The contradiction makes sense when you acknowledge that privacy and isolation are two different things. A person can want total control over where to go, when to eat, and when to return to the room — and still want company at dinner. The issue with double-occupancy pricing is that it assumes the customer brings their own company. But when only one person books, the operator has to address the pricing problem — whether or how to discount; and a product problem — how to supply a social component. Waiving a solo supplement solves the first issue, but it ignores the second. Norwegian understood this in 2010 by creating its lounge for solo travelers. The Pitch Is Easier When the Product Is for One For all these changes, travel advertising often still runs on couples: two glasses of wine, two lounge chairs, two silhouettes against a sunset. Sandals Resorts built an entire resort category around the premise. When solo travel does appear, it gets a different script. The traveler is adventurous, on a journey of self-discovery. AARP’s current solo-travel guide emphasizes personal growth and self-reliance. Even Norwegian closes its solo pitch by reassuring the reader that “you’re pretty good company.” The effect is to mark solo travel as exceptional at precisely the moment it stops being exceptional. Nobody reassures a couple that they will enjoy the balcony. Calling a solo traveler “brave” can be a compliment, but it can also reveal the assumption that traveling alone is abnormal, even when that’s changing. That all said, parts of the tourism industry have taken big steps over the past 15 years. But treating solo travelers as an audience rather than an accommodation is harder. It’s about selling them what they have already said they want: control over the trip, and access to other people, on their own terms. Marketing researchers named this opportunity in 1992. Thirty-four years later, the industry is still learning to build for one. Meanwhile, the solo traveler is standing at reception, holding a credit card, waiting for someone to design a room. items.titleOriginal: A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Τα περισσότερα οικοδομικά υλικά έχουν σχεδιαστεί για να αντέχουν τα στοιχεία, να παραμένουν σφραγισμένα και αναλλοίωτα για όσο το δυνατόν περισσότερο. Η Respyre, μια ολλανδική startup, εργάζεται από την αντίθετη αρχή. Η εταιρεία έχει αναπτύξει το Mosscrete, μια βιοδεκτική επίστρωση σκυροδέματος που δημιουργεί τις συνθήκες για να αναπτυχθούν βρύα απευθείας σε κάθετα…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre , a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete , a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology , and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. How moss takes hold Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall , which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one. The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions. Eight buildings, different tests In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one. A 300-square-meter (about 3,230-square-foot) noise barrier in Hoofddorp, the Netherlands, is being used to test passive greening: moss growing from natural moisture alone, no watering involved. The porous structure of moss may also help absorb sound, which makes the noise barrier a natural fit for the technology. A 260-square-meter (about 2,800-square-foot) social housing facade in Purmerend was one of the first practical applications. Traditional greening options were rejected there as too expensive and maintenance-heavy, and the project helped Respyre work out how bioreceptive facades are best designed and applied. In Haarlem, a 313-square-meter (about 3,370-square-foot) commercial renovation combined Mosscrete with insulation, aiming to both green the facade and improve thermal performance. Research published in June 2026 in the journal Science of the Total Environment found the effect is moisture-dependent: wet moss creates a cooling effect through evaporation, while dry moss can overheat in direct sunlight. In Amsterdam, the technology is being tested on bridge piers where graffiti has been a persistent problem. Moss-covered surfaces are less appealing as targets, and since the site has no irrigation, the project is also tracking how moss develops under ordinary conditions of rain, shade, and humidity. Designing for change Respyre is betting on a different idea of what building materials should do. Most are made to resist change, to stay gray and sealed for decades. Mosscrete is made for the opposite: it works best when moss gradually takes over. Urban greening helps manage stormwater and heat in dense cities, and there’s evidence it supports local biodiversity too. But a building slowly covered in moss doesn’t look like neglect. It looks like something is alive there. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Pumpkin spice lattes, jack-o’-lanterns, and Thanksgiving pies : pumpkins are the unofficial mascots of fall. But behind their seasonal charm lies a deeper, more complicated story that winds through language, history, agriculture, and even a little insult comedy. “ Pumpkins are more popular than ever,” says Cindy Ott , associate professor of history at the University of Delaware and author of Pumpkin: The Curious History of an American Icon. But our obsession with this humble gourd, she notes, is tied less to flavor and more to a nostalgic longing for simpler, rural times. “People are buying these things, even pumpkin spice lattes, because of these attachments, these very old-fashioned ideas about reverence of the small family farm.” A name with roots that twist like a vine The word “pumpkin” has always been more conceptual than botanical. According to Logan Kistler , curator of archaeobotany at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, the term refers to squash varieties bred to resemble the round, orange gourds we associate with fall. “Pumpkin isn’t exactly a botanical group,” he explains. Linguistically, the word has had quite a journey. Fiona McPherson of the Oxford English Dictionary traces it from the Greek pepon to the French pompon , which eventually morphed into the English “ pompion ” in the 1500s. “Pumpkin,” as we know it today, first appeared in print in 1647, ironically in reference to the meager diet of early settlers. But while the word took a European path, the plant itself is deeply American. Indigenous peoples across North, Central, and South America cultivated early pumpkin ancestors, domesticating different types of Cucurbita as far back as 10,000 years ago in Mexico. “Pumpkins are part of this genus Cucurbita,” says Kistler, noting that they were farmed widely throughout the Americas long before colonists arrived. From insult to endearment Surprisingly, it didn’t take long for the word “pumpkin” to go from dietary staple to verbal jab. By the late 1600s, it was being used as an insult. “It really did not take long for it to develop this figurative use,” says McPherson. Pumpkin became a shorthand for someone who was conceited, dim-witted, or full of hot air. Cindy Ott adds that gender played a role in the insult’s direction. For women, pumpkin imagery was linked to the body and “natural urges,” seen as a lack of refinement. For men, it implied an empty head. “It’s been used for politicians for hundreds of years,” she notes. A symbol of imagined agrarian purity By the late 19th century, the pumpkin was undergoing a cultural rehabilitation. It shifted from insult to affection, and from staple crop to nostalgic icon. “So Americans move out of the country, into the city, but they like to imagine themselves farmers at heart, many of them,” Ott explains. As industrialization transformed the U.S., the pumpkin came to symbolize the pastoral life being left behind. In poetry, paintings, and festivals, it became a stand-in for tradition and a romanticized vision of national roots. Today, that symbolism is being put to work, literally. Pumpkins are once again supporting small farmers, not as dietary staples but as attractions. Ott calls them “agrarian wonderlands,” where farms market autumnal experiences that hinge on the iconic gourd. “The cool thing about the whole story,” Ott says, “is that these very romantic ideas and myths that a lot of Americans tell themselves about their origin stories are actually helping to rejuvenate the very thing it represents: a small family farm.” Did this solution stand out?
